books.section: Topic 4.6 Market Revolution: Society and Culture, D. Gender and Family Roles in the Age of the Market Revolution

stimulus.text: Harriet Martineau, an English visitor, wrote in Society in America (1837): “If a test of civilisation be sought, none can be so sure as the condition of that half of society over which the other half has power.” She added: “The Americans have, in the treatment of women, fallen below, not only their own democratic principles, but the practice of some parts of the Old World.” Martineau also wrote that “the sum and substance of female education in America, as in England, is training women to consider marriage as the sole object in life.”
stimulus.source_note: Harriet Martineau, Society in America (1837), chapter “Woman.” Verbatim quotations verified against the Quotidiana transcription of the 1837 text.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Martineau's judgment of American treatment of women was that it

options.text: matched the democratic principles of the Declaration of Independence
options.misconception: Martineau says the opposite: Americans fell below their own democratic principles in treating women.

options.text: was the most advanced in the world
options.misconception: Martineau says America fell below even some parts of the Old World.

options.text: improved steadily as women entered factory work
options.misconception: Martineau writes about women's education and legal standing, not about factory wages improving their lot.

options.text: fell below America's own democratic principles

rationales.A: Her sentence is plain: Americans fell below their own democratic principles in the treatment of women. She does not say the treatment matched them.
rationales.B: She writes that America fell below the practice of some parts of the Old World. That is not a claim to lead the world.
rationales.C: Martineau's complaint is about education and legal standing, not about wages. Factory work is not her measure of improvement.
rationales.D: Martineau writes that Americans “have, in the treatment of women, fallen below, not only their own democratic principles, but the practice of some parts of the Old World.” Her judgment is a failure measured against America's own ideals.
rationales.general:
1. Find her verdict sentence. Americans fell below their own democratic principles.
2. Note the second half. They fell below some parts of the Old World too.
3. Keep the standard straight. She judges America by its own ideals, and finds it wanting.
Background: The Declaration promised equality, yet women could not vote, sit on juries, or hold property as wives.
Remember: a judgment that uses a country's own principles is the hardest one to answer.
